entries.1:1: This book records messages God gave to a prophet named Micah during the reigns of three kings of Judah, about the cities of Samaria and Jerusalem. It reminds us that God speaks to real people in real history, and what he says is worth listening to.
entries.1:2: God calls everyone on earth to pay attention because he is about to speak as a witness against them from his temple. It means we should take God's words seriously, since he sees and judges what we do.
entries.1:3: God is pictured as leaving his heavenly home and coming down to earth, stepping on the high places. It means God is not distant; he comes personally to deal with what happens here.
entries.1:4: When God comes, even mountains and valleys melt and crumble like wax near fire. It shows that nothing in creation can stand firm against God's power when he acts.
entries.1:5: The coming judgment is because of the sins of God's people, and the cities of Samaria and Jerusalem are named as the centers of that wrongdoing. It means religious cities are not safe if the people in them are not faithful to God.
entries.1:6: God says he will tear Samaria down until it becomes a bare field and its foundations are exposed. It means a proud city can be reduced to nothing when God judges it.
entries.1:7: Samaria's idols will be smashed and the wealth gained from idol worship will be burned up. It means things people trust instead of God will eventually be destroyed and cannot save them.
entries.1:8: Micah responds to this judgment with deep grief, weeping and going about like a mourner. It shows that someone who speaks God's truth should still feel sorrow over the harm sin brings.
entries.1:9: Samaria's wound is incurable, and the same judgment is spreading to Judah and reaching Jerusalem's gates. It means sin's damage does not stay contained; it spreads to others.
entries.1:10: Micah warns towns not to announce the disaster or weep openly, and one town is told to roll in the dust as a sign of mourning. It pictures the shame and sorrow that come with defeat.
entries.1:11: People in several towns are told to leave in shame and disgrace because their towns will be taken away. It means security in a place or a name cannot protect anyone from judgment.
entries.1:12: The people of Maroth wait anxiously for relief, but disaster from the Lord has reached Jerusalem's gates. It means hoping for good times does not help if people have not turned back to God.
entries.1:13: Lachish is told to prepare its fastest chariots, because it led Zion into sin and its example of wrongdoing spread to Israel. It means the ones who lead others into sin carry a heavy responsibility.
entries.1:14: Micah tells the people to give farewell gifts to a town that will be lost, and another town will prove deceptive to Israel's king. It means human alliances and gifts cannot be trusted to bring safety.
entries.1:15: An enemy will come and take over the town of Mareshah, and Israel's honor will be gone for good. It means no place and no pride will survive when God brings judgment.
entries.1:16: The people are told to shave their heads and mourn like an eagle losing its feathers, because their children will be taken away as captives. It means the cost of sin falls heavily on families, and grief is the right response.
entries.2:1: These people lie awake at night planning ways to do wrong, and they carry it out first thing in the morning because they have the power to do it. It warns us that planning harm when we have the power to act is itself the sin, not just the act.
entries.2:2: They greedily grab other people's land and houses by force, leaving families with nothing. It shows how wanting what belongs to others turns into cruelty against real people and their homes.
entries.2:3: God says he is planning disaster against this family that they will not be able to escape or shake off. It means God sees injustice and will act, and no amount of strength will get them out of it.
entries.2:4: A time is coming when people will sing a mocking song about them, saying their land has been taken and given to others with no way to get it back. It means those who took from others will one day lose everything themselves.
entries.2:5: When God's people gather, no one from these families will be left to measure out and assign land as their own. It means they will lose their place and share among God's people.
entries.2:6: People tell the prophets to stop saying such things, insisting that shame and disaster will never come to their family. It shows how people prefer to silence warnings rather than change their ways.
entries.2:7: They ask whether God is really so quick to anger and whether his words aren't meant to do good to those who walk uprightly. It reminds us that God's warnings are meant to help, not just to punish.
entries.2:8: You have turned against people who were at peace with you, stripping the clothes off those who pass by safely and treating them like captives of war. It means they have been attacking the innocent and defenseless instead of protecting them.
entries.2:9: You drive women away from their homes and children, and you take away the honor that belongs to their little ones forever. It means their greed is breaking up families and robbing children of what should be theirs.
entries.2:10: Get up and leave, because this place is no longer your resting place; it has been made unclean, so it will be destroyed. It means that when a place is ruined by sin, it cannot stay a safe home.
entries.2:11: If a liar came pretending to be a prophet and promised them wine and strong drink, that is exactly the kind of prophet this people would welcome. It means people who want to hear only comfortable lies will get the false teachers they prefer.
entries.2:12: God promises to gather all of Jacob and bring back the remaining Israelites, penning them together like sheep in a fold with plenty of pasture. It means that despite the judgment, God will not abandon his people but will bring them back together.
entries.2:13: The one who breaks open the way will go ahead of them, and they will break through the gate and go out, with their king and the Lord leading them. It means God himself leads his people out of captivity and opens the way to freedom.
entries.3:1: God's leaders are told to listen up, because knowing and doing what is right is their basic job. If you lead or influence others, God expects you to actually understand right from wrong.
entries.3:2: These leaders love evil and hate good, and they treat people so badly it's like tearing the skin off their bodies. It's a picture of leaders who use and destroy the people they are supposed to protect.
entries.3:3: They devour the people like meat thrown in a cooking pot, stripping them down to nothing. The point is that their cruelty is total, treating human beings as something to consume for their own benefit.
entries.3:4: When trouble comes, these leaders will cry out to God, but he won't answer them because of the evil they've done. It's a warning that God does not owe help to people who keep doing wrong and only call on him when they're in trouble.
entries.3:5: God condemns prophets who lead people astray and preach peace only to those who feed them, while threatening war on anyone who doesn't. It's a warning about leaders whose message depends on what they get paid or fed.
entries.3:6: Because of their corruption, these prophets will be left in the dark with no visions and no knowledge of what's coming. Their supposed spiritual insight will go dark, like the sun setting on them.
entries.3:7: The fortune-tellers and seers will be disgraced and confused, covering their faces in shame because God gives them no answer. People who pretend to speak for God will eventually be exposed and humiliated.
entries.3:8: In contrast, Micah says he is genuinely filled with God's Spirit, giving him power and courage to tell Israel plainly about their wrongs. It shows that true speaking for God comes with honesty about sin, not just comfort.
entries.3:9: The leaders and rulers are called to listen as ones who hate justice and twist what is straight. It's a charge against people in power who bend the truth and pervert fairness.
entries.3:10: They are building up the city through bloodshed and wrongdoing. What looks like progress or greatness is actually built on violence and injustice toward others.
entries.3:11: Judges, priests, and prophets all work for money, yet they still claim God is with them and nothing bad will happen. It exposes the danger of religious leaders who are in it for profit while pretending to have God's backing.
entries.3:12: Because of this corruption, Jerusalem will be plowed over like a field and left in ruins, and the temple mount will become like an overgrown wooded hill. It's a sober warning that God will judge a city and its worship when its leaders are deeply unjust.
entries.4:1: God's mountain—the place where he is worshipped—will be raised above everything else, and people from everywhere will stream toward it. For the reader, this is a picture of hope: God's rule will one day be the most important thing in the world, and people will be drawn to it.
entries.4:2: Many nations will urge each other to go up to God's mountain so he can teach them his ways and they can walk in his paths. It means people from all backgrounds will want to learn from God and live by what he says.
entries.4:3: God will settle disputes between powerful nations, and they will turn their weapons into farming tools and stop fighting for good. For the reader, it promises a future where war ends and God's fair decisions bring real peace.
entries.4:4: Each person will sit safely under their own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid, because God himself has promised it. It means God's peace will be personal and secure—safety and rest for ordinary people.
entries.4:5: Other peoples may follow their own gods, but God's people will keep walking in the name of the Lord their God forever. For the reader, it is a quiet commitment: whatever others do, we stay loyal to God for the long haul.
entries.4:6: God says that on that day he will gather the weak, the outcast, and those he had allowed to suffer. It means God does not forget people who feel broken or left behind—he brings them back together.
entries.4:7: The ones who stumbled will become a strong group, and God himself will rule over them as King forever. For the reader, weakness is not the end of the story; God can make the frail strong and be their king.
entries.4:8: God addresses a watchtower in Jerusalem and promises that the former rule and kingdom will come back to the city. It means God has not given up on his people's future—what was lost will be restored.
entries.4:9: The people are crying out loud as if they have no king or wise leader left, and pain has gripped them like childbirth. It means the question is asked: why despair, when God has not abandoned you?
entries.4:10: Zion is told to writhe in pain because she will be taken out of the city, live in open country, and go as far as Babylon—but there God will rescue her. For the reader, hard exile is real, yet God promises freedom even in the worst place.
entries.4:11: Many nations have gathered against Zion, wanting to see her disgraced and ruined. It means God's people face real enemies who want them to fall, and the pressure feels overwhelming.
entries.4:12: Those nations don't understand God's plans; they don't realize he has gathered them like grain to be threshed. For the reader, enemies may think they are winning, but God's purpose is hidden from them and he is still in control.
entries.4:13: Zion is told to rise and thresh, because God will make her strong like iron and bronze, and she will dedicate the wealth of defeated peoples to the Lord. It means God can turn a weak, oppressed people into a strong instrument of his justice.
entries.5:1: Israel's leaders are being humiliated and struck in the face while the city is under siege. It means God's people face hard consequences for their failure, and it warns readers that leaders who ignore God will be brought low.
entries.5:2: God promises a ruler will come from Bethlehem, a small and unimportant town, and this ruler's origin goes back to ancient, eternal times. It means God often works through the small and overlooked, and it points readers to hope in a leader God himself provides.
entries.5:3: God will leave his people to their troubles until the promised child is born, and then the rest of the family will return. It means waiting is part of God's plan, and readers can trust that God's promise will come at the right time.
entries.5:4: The coming ruler will care for his people like a shepherd, strong in the Lord, and they will live safely because his greatness reaches everywhere. It means good leadership protects and feeds people, and readers can rest secure under a ruler who relies on God.
entries.5:5: This ruler will bring peace, and when a powerful enemy invades, plenty of capable leaders will rise up to defend the people. It means God gives peace and raises up helpers in times of threat, so readers need not face danger alone.
entries.5:6: These leaders will defeat Assyria and the land of Nimrod and rescue God's people from the invader. It means God defends his people against overwhelming enemies, and readers can trust him to deliver them.
entries.5:7: The surviving people of God will be like dew and rain among the nations, bringing fresh life that no one can hold back. It means God's people are meant to quietly bless those around them, and readers should see their presence as life-giving to others.
entries.5:8: Among the nations God's people will be like a lion that cannot be stopped, crushing any who oppose them. It means God gives his people real strength against their enemies, and readers should not mistake his people for helpless.
entries.5:9: God's hand will be raised against the enemies of his people, and all who hate them will be removed. It means God takes sides against those who oppose his people, and readers can trust him to deal with their enemies.
entries.5:10: God says he will take away the horses and destroy the war chariots his people rely on. It means God strips away false sources of security, and readers are reminded not to trust in military strength or their own resources.
entries.5:11: God will tear down the towns and strong fortresses his people trust in. It means human defenses cannot replace trust in God, and readers should not put their confidence in walls or weapons.
entries.5:12: God will end the practice of secret arts and fortune-telling among his people. It means God wants undivided loyalty, and readers should not look to magic or superstition for guidance.
entries.5:13: God will remove the carved images and sacred pillars his people worship and stop them bowing to things they made with their own hands. It means idolatry must go, and readers should examine what they have made into a god.
entries.5:14: God will pull up the Asherah poles and destroy the idols among his people. It means God will not tolerate rival objects of worship, and readers are called to clear out anything that takes his place.
entries.5:15: God will punish the nations in fierce anger, something they never expected. It means God's judgment is real and will fall on those who oppose him, and readers should take his warnings seriously.
entries.6:1: God is telling His people to listen and to state their case, with the mountains and hills as witnesses. It means God invites us to bring our complaints honestly before Him rather than grumble behind His back.
entries.6:2: God calls the mountains and the foundations of the earth to witness a dispute He has with His own people. It means God takes His relationship with us seriously enough to press charges when we go wrong.
entries.6:3: God asks His people what He has done to tire them out or make them turn away. It means God wants us to see that any distance between us and Him is not because He failed us.
entries.6:4: God reminds them He rescued them from slavery in Egypt and sent leaders to guide them. It means remembering God's past kindness helps us trust Him instead of resenting Him.
entries.6:5: God recalls how He protected them from a king's curse and brought them safely into the land. It means God's faithful acts in the past are reasons to trust His goodness now.
entries.6:6: The people ask what grand offering would be enough to approach God with proper respect. It means we often think we can earn God's favor with impressive gifts, but that misses what He actually wants.
entries.6:7: They wonder if huge amounts of animals or even a child sacrifice could pay for their sin. It means no price we could pay can buy off our guilt; God is not looking for a transaction.
entries.6:8: God has told you what he wants: act justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Simple to say, and harder than it sounds.
entries.6:9: God's voice calls out to the city and its people to listen to what He is saying. It means God still speaks to whole communities and expects them to pay attention.
entries.6:10: God asks whether He should ignore dishonest wealth and cheating in the marketplace. It means God sees how we get our money and does not overlook crooked dealings.
entries.6:11: God asks whether He can simply let rigged scales and fake weights go unpunished. It means cheating others in business matters to God and will not be shrugged off.
entries.6:12: The rich are violent, and the people lie and deceive with their words. It means a society that runs on greed and dishonesty is one God will hold accountable.
entries.6:13: God says He has begun to bring punishment and ruin on them because of their sins. It means sin has real consequences, and God does not let it continue without response.
entries.6:14: They will eat but stay hungry, and whatever they save will not be safe. It means when we chase gain dishonestly, we end up empty and insecure anyway.
entries.6:15: They will plant, press olives, and harvest grapes but get no grain, oil, or wine. It means hard work without God's blessing produces nothing lasting.
entries.6:16: They followed the corrupt ways of earlier kings, so God will make them a warning and a disgrace. It means copying bad examples leads to shame, and God's people are meant to be different.
entries.7:1: The prophet feels like a hungry person who finds the harvest already picked and no fruit left to eat. He is saying that good people and good things have disappeared from his world, and we can feel that same grief when goodness seems gone around us.
entries.7:2: Faithful people have vanished from the land, and everyone is out to harm others, even their own family. It means we should not be surprised when trust is hard to find, and we should guard our own honesty.
entries.7:3: People in power use their hands to do wrong: rulers demand money, judges want bribes, and important men decide whatever suits them. It reminds us that corruption in leadership hurts everyone, and we should not admire power that twists what is right.
entries.7:4: Even the best people are like a thorny hedge that tears you when you touch it. The prophet warns that a day of reckoning is coming, so we should take wrongdoing seriously rather than pretend it is fine.
entries.7:5: Do not fully trust even a close friend or relative, and be careful what you say to the person closest to you. It means loyalty can fail, so we should be wise and watch our words while still loving people.
entries.7:6: Family members turn against each other, with children shaming parents and in-laws fighting. It describes how broken relationships can get, and it warns us that even home may not be safe when people stop honoring each other.
entries.7:7: In contrast to all that betrayal, the prophet chooses to look to the Lord and wait for God to save him. It means when people let us down, we can still put our hope in God and trust that he hears us.
entries.7:8: The prophet tells his enemy not to celebrate his downfall, because he will rise again and the Lord will be his light in the darkness. It means our troubles are not the end of the story when God is with us.
entries.7:9: He accepts God's discipline for his sin and waits for God to defend his case and bring him into the light. It means we can accept correction humbly, trusting that God's discipline is meant to restore us, not destroy us.
entries.7:10: The enemy who mocked him will see God act and be ashamed, and she will be trampled like street dust. It means God will eventually set things right, so we do not need to take revenge ourselves.
entries.7:11: A day is coming when the walls will be rebuilt and the city's boundaries will spread wide. It means after judgment God restores and enlarges his people, giving hope that ruin is not the final word.
entries.7:12: People will come from faraway places like Assyria and Egypt, from sea to sea and mountain to mountain. It means God's restored people will draw others in from everywhere, showing that his welcome reaches beyond one nation.
entries.7:13: The land will be laid waste because of the evil its people have done. It means sin has real consequences on the ground we live on, and we should not think our actions only affect ourselves.
entries.7:14: The prophet asks God to shepherd his people like a flock with his staff, feeding them in rich pasture as in the old days. It means we can ask God to care for and provide for us, trusting him as a shepherd cares for sheep.
entries.7:15: He asks God to show wonders again, just as he did when he brought Israel out of Egypt. It means we can pray for God to act powerfully in our day, remembering what he has done before.
entries.7:16: The nations will see God's power and be ashamed, covering their mouths and stopping their ears in silence. It means God's actions will silence those who boasted against him, and we should humble ourselves before him.
entries.7:17: They will crawl in the dust like snakes and come trembling out of their hiding places to the Lord our God. It means even proud enemies will end up bowing in fear, so it is better to come to God humbly now.
entries.7:18: The prophet praises God for being unlike any other, forgiving sin and not staying angry forever because he delights in mercy. It means God's greatest joy is to show mercy, so we can bring our failures to him without despair.
entries.7:19: God will have compassion again, trample our sins underfoot, and throw them into the depths of the sea. It means God does not just forgive a little; he removes our guilt completely and remembers it no more.
entries.7:20: God will keep the faithful promises he swore long ago to Jacob and Abraham. It means God's mercy is reliable because he keeps his word, and we can count on him to be faithful to us too.
